Simulations reveal that a rapid decrease in the overlying field strength with height, characteristic of complex active regions, leads to impulsive accelerations and fast CMEs. In contrast, a gentler field decay, typical of quiet-Sun regions, results in gradual accelerations and slow CMEs. The eruption dynamics are governed primarily by the torus instability, where the decay index of the external field determines the onset and profile of the acceleration. These results confirm that fast and slow CMEs can be described uniformly through variations in the background magnetic field topology, without requiring distinct initiation mechanisms. The simulated CMEs reproduce observed kinematic profiles and highlight the role of magnetic reconfiguration in driving the eruptions.
label: llm

text: We investigate the dynamical properties of asymmetric nuclear matter at lowdensity. The occurrence of new instabilities, that lead the system to adynamical fragment formation, is illustrated, discussing in particular thecharge symmetry dependence of the structure of the most important unstablemodes. We observe that instabilities are reduced by charge asymmetry, leadingto larger size and time scales in the fragmentation process. Configurationswith less asymmetric fragments surrounded by a more asymmetric gas arefavoured. Interesting variances with respect to a pure thermodynamicalprediction are revealed, that can be checked experimentally. All these featuresare deeply related to the structure of the symmetry term in the nuclearEquation of State (EOS) and could be used to extract information on the lowdensity part of the EOS.
label: human

text: We investigate the spinodal decomposition process in low-density asymmetric nuclear matter, where mechanical instabilities drive the system toward a liquid-gas phase separation. At subsaturation densities, the presence of isospin asymmetry modifies the instability region, leading to a single dominant isoscalar-like unstable mode that favors density fluctuations over pure isovector ones. This instability directs the phase separation toward restoring isospin symmetry in the denser (liquid) phase while enhancing asymmetry in the rarer (gas) phase, a phenomenon known as isospin fractionation or distillation. The growth rates of unstable modes and the resulting cluster sizes are influenced by the nuclear symmetry energy, which plays a critical role in determining the boundaries of the spinodal region. Quantum statistical effects further shift dominant wavelengths and amplify fluctuations, particularly at lower temperatures.
label: llm

text: Crosslinks and molecular motors play an important role in the organization ofcytoskeletal filament networks. Here we incorporate the effect of crosslinksinto our model of polar motor-filament organization [Phys. Rev. E {\bf 71},050901 (2005)], through suppressing the relative sliding of filaments in thecourse of motor-mediated alignment. We show that this modification leads to anontrivial macroscopic behavior, namely the oriented state exhibits atransverse instability in contrast to the isotropic instability that occurswithout crosslinks. This transverse instability leads to the formation of denseextended bundles of oriented filaments, similar to recently observed structuresin actomyosin. This model also can be applied to situations with two oppositelydirected motor species or motors with different processing speeds.
label: human

text: Active cytoskeletal networks, composed of polar filaments and molecular motors, exhibit emergent self-organization driven by motor activity. Crosslinking proteins play a critical role in modulating this process by influencing filament connectivity and alignment. In motor-mediated systems, passive crosslinks enhance network rigidity, facilitating the transmission of motor-generated forces across larger scales. At low crosslink densities, motors promote extensile stresses and filament sliding, leading to disordered or expansive configurations. Higher crosslink concentrations enable buckling and polarity sorting, transitioning the network toward contractile states with bundled structures. Computational and in vitro studies reveal that crosslink density qualitatively alters motor-driven deformation modes, from extensile to contractile.
label: llm

text: We investigate non-perturbative features of a three-dimensional Abelian Higgsmodel with singly- and doubly-charged scalar fields coupled to a single compactAbelian gauge field. The model is pretending to describe various planar systemsof strongly correlated electrons such as high-Tc superconductivity in theoverdoped regime and exotic materials possessing excitations withfractionalized quantum numbers. The complicated phase structure of the model isstudied thoroughly using numerical tools and analytical arguments. In thethree-dimensional space of coupling parameters we identify the Fermi liquid,the spin gap, the superconductor and the strange metallic phases. The behaviorof three kinds of topological defects -- holon and spinon vortices andmonopoles - is explored in various phases. We also observe a new effect, thestrong enhancement of the phase transition strength reflected in a lower orderof the transition: at sufficiently strong gauge coupling the two second orderphase transitions -- corresponding to spinon-pair and holon condensation lines- join partially in the phase diagram and become a first order phase transitionin that region. The last observation may have an analogue in QuantumChromodynamics at non-zero temperature and finite baryon density. We argue thatat sufficiently large baryon density the finite-temperature transition betweenthe (3-flavor paired) color superconducting phase and the quark-gluon plasmaphases should be much stronger compared with the transition between 2-flavorpaired and 3-flavor paired superconducting phases.
label: human

text: We investigate nonperturbative features of a three-dimensional compact Abelian Higgs model featuring singly and doubly charged scalar fields coupled to a single Abelian gauge field. This model serves as an effective description for planar systems of strongly correlated electrons, including high-temperature superconductivity in the overdoped regime and materials exhibiting fractionalized excitations such as spinons and holons. The phase structure is explored using a combination of numerical Monte Carlo simulations and analytical arguments. The phase diagram reveals multiple regions corresponding to distinct condensates: holon condensation, spinon-pair condensation, and coexisting phases. At weak gauge couplings, the transitions associated with these condensates are second-order. However, at sufficiently strong gauge couplings, the two second-order transition lines partially merge, resulting in a segment of first-order phase transition. This strengthening of the transition order reflects enhanced nonperturbative effects mediated by the gauge field. Finally, we discuss potential analogies to quantum chromodynamics at finite baryon density, where similar gauge-mediated mechanisms may intensify the transition between color-superconducting phases and the quark-gluon plasma.
label: llm

text: The well known FPU phenomenon (lack of attainment of equipartition of themode--energies at low energies, for some exceptional initial data) suggeststhat the FPU model does not have the mixing property at low energies. We givenumerical indications that this is actually the case. This we show by computingorbits for sets of initial data of full measure, sampled out from themicrocanonical ensemble by standard Montecarlo techniques. Mixing is tested bylooking at the decay of the autocorrelations of the mode--energies, and it isfound that the high--frequency modes have autocorrelations that tend instead topositive values. Indications are given that such a nonmixing property survivesin the thermodynamic limit. It is left as an open problem whether mixingobtains within time--scales much longer than the presently available ones.
label: human

text: The well-known Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) phenomenon, originally observed for exceptional initial excitations of low-frequency modes, consists in the lack of equipartition among normal mode energies at low specific energies. This work investigates whether an analogous phenomenon persists for generic initial data, sampled from the Gibbs measure at low temperature, rather than special excitations of zero measure. Numerical simulations are performed on the FPU-β model with a large number of oscillators, averaging the time evolution of mode energies over many initial conditions. The results reveal a persistent sharing of energy primarily among lower-frequency modes, with higher modes remaining weakly excited on observable timescales. This behavior indicates the presence of a metastable state and suggests that the system lacks strong mixing properties in the low-energy regime.
label: llm

text: We revisit the model of a system made up of a Brownian quantum oscillatorunder the influence of an external classical force and linearly coupled to anenvironment made up of many quantum oscillators at zero or finite temperature.We show that the HPZ master equation for the reduced density matrix derivedearlier [B.L. Hu, J.P. Paz, Y. Zhang, Phys. Rev. D 45, 2843 (1992)] withcoefficients obtained from solutions of integro-differential equations canassume closed functional forms for a fairly general class of spectral densitiesof the environment at arbitrary temperature and coupling strength. As anillustration of these new results we solve the corresponding master equationand calculate, among other physical quantities, the uncertainty function whoselate time behavior can be obtained fully. This produces a formula forinvestigating the standard quantum limit which is central to addressing manytheoretical issues in macroscopic quantum phenomena and experimental concernsrelated to low temperature precision measurements. We find that any initialstate always settles down to a Gaussian density matrix whose covariance isdetermined by the thermal reservoir and whose mean is determined by theexternal force. For more general spectra we show that the solution of themaster equation can be reduced to solving for the motion of a classicalparametric oscillator with parametric frequency determined by the unsolved formaster equation coefficients. States in these systems experience evolution thatis parametrically similar to the simpler evolution explicitly determined for inthe case of Laurent-series spectra.
label: human

text: We revisit the quantum Brownian motion of a harmonic oscillator subjected to an external classical force and linearly coupled to a general bath of harmonic oscillators at arbitrary temperature. The exact Hu-Paz-Zhang (HPZ) master equation for the reduced density matrix, originally derived with time-dependent coefficients from integro-differential equations, is shown to admit closed functional forms for a broad class of environmental spectral densities. These closed forms hold independently of temperature and coupling strength, extending prior results limited to specific cases. The inclusion of an external force introduces a driving term that shifts the mean position without altering the dissipative or diffusive coefficients. We derive explicit solutions for the time evolution of the reduced density matrix, revealing that arbitrary initial states evolve toward a Gaussian form in the long-time limit. The equilibrium covariance matrix is fully determined by the thermal fluctuations of the bath, satisfying the quantum fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The mean values of position and momentum follow classical trajectories driven by the external force, damped by the environment. For certain spectral densities, the master equation coefficients are obtained analytically via contour integration, yielding exact expressions for renormalization, dissipation, and diffusion terms. These solutions provide insight into macroscopic quantum phenomena, including the quantum limit of precision measurements and decoherence processes under driven conditions.
label: llm

text: This paper investigates the use of evolutionary optimisation techniques toregister a template with a scene image. An error function is created to measurethe correspondence of the template to the image. The problem presented here isto optimise the horizontal, vertical and scaling parameters that register thetemplate with the scene. The Genetic Algorithm, Simulated Annealing andParticle Swarm Optimisations are compared to a Nelder-Mead Simplex optimisationwith starting points chosen in a pre-processing stage. The paper investigatesthe precision and accuracy of each method and shows that all four methodsperform favourably for image registration. SA is the most precise, GA is themost accurate. PSO is a good mix of both and the Simplex method returns localminima the most. A pre-processing stage should be investigated for theevolutionary methods in order to improve performance. Discrete versions of theoptimisation methods should be investigated to further improve computationalperformance.
label: human

text: Template-based image registration involves aligning a predefined template image with a target scene image by optimizing transformation parameters to maximize correspondence. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with multimodal fitness landscapes and local optima in such registration tasks. Evolutionary optimization techniques offer robust global search capabilities, making them suitable for addressing these challenges. This study explores the application of evolutionary methods, including Genetic Algorithms (GA), Simulated Annealing (SA), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), to template-based registration. An error function based on pixel intensity differences is employed as the fitness metric to evaluate alignment quality. The optimization focuses on key parameters such as horizontal translation, vertical translation, and uniform scaling. Comparisons are made with the classical Nelder-Mead Simplex method, which uses pre-processed initial points for local refinement. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that all tested methods achieve favorable registration performance on various image pairs.

text: We describe our software package Block Locally Optimal PreconditionedEigenvalue Xolvers (BLOPEX) publicly released recently. BLOPEX is available asa stand-alone serial library, as an external package to PETSc (``Portable,Extensible Toolkit for Scientific Computation'', a general purpose suite oftools for the scalable solution of partial differential equations and relatedproblems developed by Argonne National Laboratory), and is also built into {\ithypre} (``High Performance Preconditioners'', scalable linear solvers packagedeveloped by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory). The present BLOPEXrelease includes only one solver--the Locally Optimal Block PreconditionedConjugate Gradient (LOBPCG) method for symmetric eigenvalue problems. {\ithypre} provides users with advanced high-quality parallel preconditioners forlinear systems, in particular, with domain decomposition and multigridpreconditioners. With BLOPEX, the same preconditioners can now be efficientlyused for symmetric eigenvalue problems. PETSc facilitates the integration ofindependently developed application modules with strict attention to componentinteroperability, and makes BLOPEX extremely easy to compile and use withpreconditioners that are available via PETSc. We present the LOBPCG algorithmin BLOPEX for {\it hypre} and PETSc. We demonstrate numerically the scalabilityof BLOPEX by testing it on a number of distributed and shared memory parallelsystems, including a Beowulf system, SUN Fire 880, an AMD dual-core Opteronworkstation, and IBM BlueGene/L supercomputer, using PETSc domain decompositionand {\it hypre} multigrid preconditioning. We test BLOPEX on a model problem,the standard 7-point finite-difference approximation of the 3-D Laplacian, withthe problem size in the range $10^5-10^8$.

text: This paper introduces Block Locally Optimal Preconditioned Eigenvalue Xolvers (BLOPEX), a software package designed for solving large-scale symmetric eigenvalue problems using preconditioned iterative methods. BLOPEX is available in multiple forms: as a stand-alone serial library, as an external package integrated with PETSc, and built directly into the hypre library. The core solver implemented in the current release is the Locally Optimal Block Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (LOBPCG) method, which is particularly effective for computing extreme eigenpairs of symmetric positive definite generalized eigenvalue problems. The integration with hypre enables the direct reuse of its high-quality parallel multigrid and domain decomposition preconditioners, originally developed for linear systems, now applied efficiently to eigenvalue computations. Similarly, the PETSc interface leverages PETSc's modular design to facilitate seamless interoperability with a wide range of existing preconditioners and parallel computing tools. The abstract implementation of LOBPCG in BLOPEX allows for flexible deployment across different software environments through user-supplied operator interfaces. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scalability of BLOPEX on various parallel architectures, including shared-memory systems and distributed clusters. Tests on a model problem—the 7-point finite-difference discretization of the 3D Laplacian with problem sizes ranging from 10^5 to 10^8 degrees of freedom—confirm strong scaling when using hypre multigrid and PETSc domain decomposition preconditioning. Overall, BLOPEX provides a robust and efficient framework for preconditioned eigensolving in high-performance scientific computing applications.

text: Electron acceleration in high Mach number perpendicular shocks isinvestigated through two-dimensional electrostatic particle-in-cell (PIC)simulation. In contrast to previous one-dimensional simulations in which strongsurfing acceleration is realized, we find that surfing acceleration does notoccur in two-dimensional simulation. This is because excited electrostaticpotentials have a two-dimensional structure that makes electron trappingimpossible. Thus, the surfing acceleration does not work either in itself or asan injection mechanism for the diffusive shock acceleration. We briefly discussimplications of the present results on the electron heating and acceleration byshocks in supernova remnants.

text: Electron acceleration in high Mach number perpendicular collisionless shocks is investigated using a two-dimensional electrostatic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation focused on the shock foot region. The simulation initializes particles comprising incident protons and electrons along with reflected protons, establishing conditions conducive to the Buneman instability. In contrast to prior one-dimensional simulations where robust electron surfing acceleration was observed, the two-dimensional setup reveals no significant surfing acceleration of electrons. This absence arises because the excited electrostatic potentials develop a complex two-dimensional structure. Such multidimensional potential configurations prevent effective long-term trapping of electrons within the wave structures. Consequently, electron surfing acceleration proves ineffective both as a standalone mechanism and as a potential injection process for subsequent diffusive shock acceleration in realistic multidimensional shock environments.

text: As the dimensionality is reduced, the world becomes more and moreinteresting; novel and fascinating phenomena show up which call forunderstanding. Physics in one dimension is a fascinating topic for theory andexperiment: for the former often a simplification, for the latter always achallenge. Various ways will be demonstrated how one-dimensional structures canbe achieved in reality. In particular organic conductors could establishthemselves as model systems for the investigation of the physics in reduceddimensions.  In the metallic state of a one-dimensional solid, Fermi-liquid theory breaksdown and spin and charge degrees of freedom become separated. But the metallicphase is not stable in one dimension: as the temperature is reduced, theelectronic charge and spin tend to arrange themselves in an ordered fashion dueto strong correlations. The competition of the different interactions isresponsible for which broken-symmetry ground state is eventually realized in aspecific compound and which drives the system towards an insulating state.  Here we review the various ordering phenomena and how they can be identifiedby dielectric and optic measurements.

text: One-dimensional solids exhibit fascinating electronic properties due to reduced dimensionality, where strong electron correlations and electron-phonon interactions play dominant roles. In these systems, the metallic phase is inherently unstable at low temperatures, leading to various broken-symmetry ground states. Charge-ordering phenomena arise from the tendency of electrons to arrange in periodic patterns, often driven by Coulomb repulsion or nesting of the Fermi surface. A key example is the charge density wave (CDW), originating from the Peierls instability, where a periodic lattice distortion opens a gap at the Fermi level, stabilizing an insulating state. In contrast, charge ordering in correlated systems, such as quarter-filled organic conductors, results from short-range Coulomb interactions localizing charges on specific sites, forming patterns like Wigner crystals or stripes. These mechanisms can compete or coexist, with the dominant one determined by the balance of electron-electron repulsion, electron-phonon coupling, and bandwidth. Optical and dielectric spectroscopy provide powerful tools to distinguish CDW from pure charge-ordered states, revealing differences in gap formation and collective excitations.

text: We propose a new field-theoretic framework for formulating thenon-relativistic quantum mechanics of D particles in a Fock space of U(N)Yang-Mills theories with all different N in a unified way. D-particle fieldoperators, creating and annihilating a D particle and hence changing N one byone, are defined. The base space of these D-particle fields is a (complex)vector space of infinite dimensions. The gauge invariance of Yang-Mills quantummechanics is reinterpreted as a quantum-statistical symmetry, which is takeninto account by setting up a novel algebraic and projective structure in theformalism. Ordinary physical observables of Yang-Mills theory, obeying thestandard algebra, are expressed as bilinear forms of the D-particle fields.Together with the open-closed string duality, our new formulation suggests atrinity of three different but mutually dual viewpoints in string theory.

These fields are defined over an infinite-dimensional complex vector space as their base manifold. The inherent gauge invariance of Yang-Mills quantum mechanics is reinterpreted as a quantum-statistical symmetry, accommodated through a specialized algebraic and projective structure in the formalism. Finally, standard physical observables of the Yang-Mills theory, satisfying conventional algebraic relations, are constructed as bilinear expressions in terms of these D-particle fields.

text: The four-dimensional Eigenvector 1 (4DE1) parameter space provides a powerful framework for organizing the spectroscopic diversity observed in broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN). This space is primarily driven by the Eddington ratio, with secondary contributions from source orientation effects. Key optical parameters in 4DE1 include the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the broad Hβ emission line and the strength of the optical Fe II emission blend relative to Hβ (R_FeII). The high-ionization C IV λ1549 emission line has emerged as a critical ultraviolet diagnostic within this context. This study utilizes high signal-to-noise Hubble Space Telescope (HST) archival spectra of 130 AGN to measure reliable broad component properties of C IV λ1549. Systematic blueshifts in the C IV λ1549 broad profile are predominantly found in sources with FWHM(Hβ) < 4000 km s⁻¹, designated as Population A. Population A sources are largely radio-quiet and include narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, though the latter do not form a distinct subclass. No significant blueshifts are observed in broader-lined sources (FWHM(Hβ) > 4000 km s⁻¹), termed Population B, which encompass most radio-loud AGN. These blueshifts are interpreted as signatures of disk winds or outflows driven by high accretion rates. New correlations are identified between the FWHM of the C IV λ1549 broad component and its line shift amplitude. Additional correlations involve the equivalent width of C IV λ1549 and other 4DE1 parameters. Population A sources exhibit stronger correlations, consistent with higher Eddington ratios promoting outflow activity. The dichotomy between Populations A and B appears more fundamental to broad-line region structure than the traditional radio-loud versus radio-quiet classification.

text: We present deep polarimetric observations at 1420 MHz of the European Large Area ISO Survey North 1 region (ELAIS N1) as part of the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory Planck Deep Fields project. By combining closely spaced aperture synthesis fields, we image a region of 7.43 square degrees to a maximum sensitivity in Stokes Q and U of 78 μJy beam⁻¹. This value is approximately three times higher than that observed for sources exceeding 100 mJy in total intensity. text: In any attempt to build a quantum theory of gravity, a central issue is tounravel the structure of space-time at the smallest scale. Of particularrelevance is the possible definition of coordinate functions within the theoryand the study of their algebraic properties, such as non-commutativity. Here weapproach this issue from the perspective of loop quantum gravity and thepicture of quantum geometry that the formalism offers. In particular, as weargue here, this emerging picture has two main elements: i) The nature of thequantum geometry at Planck scale is one-dimensional, polymeric with quantizedgeometrical quantities and; ii) Appropriately defined operators correspondingto coordinates by means of intrinsic, relational, constructions becomenon-commuting. This particular feature of the operators, that operationallylocalize points on space, gives rise to an emerging geometry that is also, in aprecise sense, fuzzy.

text: In quantum gravity theories, understanding the microstructure of spacetime at Planck scales is crucial, particularly through the potential definition of coordinate operators and their algebraic relations, including non-commutativity. We construct operators intended to localize points in space and analyze their properties within the kinematical Hilbert space. These operators exhibit characteristics that prevent sharp localization, resulting in an inherent uncertainty. Consequently, the emergent quantum geometry is not only discrete but also fuzzy in a precise operational sense, with implications for the classical limit and semiclassical states.

text: The charmless hadronic decays of $B_{s}$ and $B_{d}$ mesons into $\pi\pi$, $\pi K$, and $KK$ final states provide a rich laboratory for probing CP violation and extracting the CKM angle $\gamma$ through U-spin symmetry relations. These modes, particularly the pairs $B_d\to\pi^+\pi^-$ with $B_s\to K^+K^-$ and $B_d\to\pi^\mp K^\pm$ with $B_s\to\pi^\pm K^\mp$, allow complementary strategies to determine $\gamma$ while controlling penguin contributions. Recent high-precision measurements from LHCb have significantly improved branching ratios and CP asymmetries, largely resolving earlier tensions such as the "$\pi K$ puzzle" and aligning observables closer to Standard Model expectations. U-spin-breaking effects remain moderate, enabling robust extractions of $\gamma$ with reduced theoretical uncertainties. Time-dependent analyses of $B_s\to K^+K^-$ have yielded precise determinations of the $B_s$ mixing phase and mixing-induced CP violation. Future data from LHCb upgrades and Belle II are expected to further constrain potential new physics contributions in electroweak penguins and refine the full exploitation of these channels for CKM metrology.

A drop lands on the paper anyway, smudging one circle. I laugh once, quietly, because crying in a voting booth is so predictably human. The names blur into a single long accusation. Yet, looking back through the myths of ancient' Earth', it becomes clear. Take Tithonus or Europa. Their history is full of legends of those who would fuck the literal manifestations of the sun and stars, the earth and sky. Is it any surprise they are who they are? When humans found that they could not, in fact fuck the sky, they turned to the next best thing. No denizen of space is safe from human attraction, even when it would seem a physical impossibility. This is a species that invented Viagra decades before they cured cancer, if they had to invent a machine to fuck something, that machine got invented. And they are good. In fact, during the Lorath-Gl' r' qk War, the Lorathi introduced humans to the home world of the murderously monogamous Gl' r' qk as an attack on their psyche, this caused the almost total collapse of Gl' r' qk society as the most of the planet was engulfed in honour-bound blood duels. To this day, humanity is the only species to have won an interstellar war with their genitals. This is also historically significant for blurring the line between mercenary and prostitute when it comes to humans. Now, most species do not regard sex with humans as an act of infidelity, and the ability to retain a personal human courtesan is a status symbol greater than owning one of their fusion drives. No settlement without brothels filled with humans could ever be taken seriously, and millions of new Tithonus' s drift amongst their beloved stars.

text: In the vast tapestry of the Galactic Concordance, humanity was universally regarded as the bumbling newcomer, a species that stumbled into interstellar society like a toddler into a formal banquet. Other races mastered quantum engineering before they discovered fire, while humans still struggled with basic warp stabilization centuries after first contact. The avian Sylari could navigate hyperspace lanes with instinctive precision that made human pilots look like drunkards behind the wheel. The crustacean Vorrn built megastructures that spanned star systems, laughing at humanity's fragile space stations that required constant repairs. Even in diplomacy, the telepathic Lirans wove alliances with effortless empathy, whereas human negotiators often offended entire delegations with misplaced humor or blunt honesty. Biologically, humans were frail: shorter lifespans, weaker bones, and no natural defenses compared to the armored hides or regenerative abilities of others. In art, music, and philosophy, alien civilizations produced symphonies that reshaped reality and treatises that predicted cosmic events, leaving human creations seeming primitive and chaotic. Yet, there was one domain where humanity shone with an unnatural, almost terrifying brilliance: improvisation under impossible constraints. When a Vorrn dreadnought's core breached near a neutral colony, every expert race froze in protocol paralysis, but a human engineer jury-rigged a fix using scrap metal and chewing gum, saving millions. During the Great Silence outbreak—a virus that jammed all known communication tech—the Sylari and Lirans despaired, but humans rediscovered ancient acoustic signaling and smoke patterns to coordinate a galaxy-wide resistance. In warfare simulations, alien fleets adhered to flawless strategies that crumbled when human commanders threw randomness into the mix, turning predictable battles into chaotic victories.
label: llm

text: 1. Back in middle school, I used to laugh at those chain texts promising that a ghostly girl in a white dress would appear by my bed if I didn't forward the message to ten people within an hour. 2. I'd delete them immediately, rolling my eyes at how gullible people were, convinced they were just silly hoaxes designed to spread panic. 3. Years later, on a quiet December night in 2025, I found an old phone in a drawer and, out of nostalgia, scrolled through the archived messages. 4. One unread chain text from 2012 glowed on the screen, its warning identical to the ones I remembered: "She is real. Forward this or she will stand beside you tonight." 5. I smirked, remembering how I'd ignored dozens just like it, and closed the phone without a second thought. 6. That night, as I lay in bed scrolling on my new phone, the room grew unnaturally cold, though the window was shut tight. 7. A faint creak sounded from the floorboards near the foot of my bed, but when I looked, nothing was there. 8. Hours passed in restless half-sleep until, just before dawn, I felt an unmistakable presence—like someone standing silently, watching me breathe. 9. Heart pounding, I turned on the light to find no one, yet the chill lingered and my old phone, across the room, buzzed once with a new notification. 10. Trembling, I opened it to see the same chain text resent, timestamped moments ago, with an added line: "I told you they were all real." 11. Now, every ignored message from the past feels like a debt unpaid, and I swear sometimes, in the corner of my eye, a pale figure in white waits patiently for the night I finally look directly at her.
label: llm

text: Dear Robin, Wow. Quite an interesting thing how something as beautiful as a star ends with something as devastating as a black-hole. That was us... we were light, then we were dark. I often find myself coercing my brain to hate you. I want to hate you, because if I do n' t, I acknowledge how *bad* it was. I acknowledge how bad I made it. You, you beautiful broken masterpiece, you deserved nothing of what I gave you. You, you suicidal manic eloquent angel, you should have taken off for the hills. You should have flew, Robin. Looking back I' m sure you hate me more than anyone alive, I ca n' t blame you. After I held your hand as he died of cancer, after I recreated you from the scattered pieces that was your confidence, the wholeness of you weighed like a burden on my shoulders. You were no longer a fascination, you were a scar that placed itself at my side, one I could not erase out of pity. I pitied you, and in my flawed attempts to protect you from the evil of this world, I destroyed you. I could never face you... I hope you' ve learned from the experience of me. You' ve taught me what I' m capable of. -Yours

text: Dear [Ex's Name], I hope this letter finds you well, though I know you probably weren't expecting to hear from me again. It's been exactly two years since that rainy afternoon when we said goodbye on the corner of Elm Street. Some days, the silence between us feels heavier than any argument we ever had. I still catch myself reaching for my phone to share a stupid meme, only to remember you're no longer there. The coffee shop we used to call "ours" changed its menu, and I hated it at first because it felt like another piece of us erased. I've learned that missing someone isn't a straight line—it curves, it dips, it surprises you in quiet moments. There were nights I replayed every harsh word I said, wishing I could swallow them back. I've grown enough to admit I wasn't always the partner you deserved. Watching you walk away that day broke something in me I didn't know could break. Yet somehow, the pieces have slowly rearranged into a version of myself I actually recognize. I don't write this hoping you'll come back; I know that's not what either of us needs. I just needed you to know that the love we shared wasn't wasted—it shaped me in ways I'm grateful for.
label: llm

text: " What happened? " I asked them. Silence. Awkward faces. " Anybody? " They looked troubled. Sad. " Richard... " some of them said. " Yes? " I answered, but they did n' t say anything more, only shook their heads. It was 76 days since the last accident, when a hammer fell from the third floor of south building and crushed Miguel' s thumb to dust. *76 days since last accident*, that' s what the sign said - and it was almost true: hard stuff of various kinds hitting helmets or steel-toed boots happened regularly, and were n' t counted as accidents. Also, no one was wuss enough to report a minor cut or bruise as an accident. We took pride in the fact that we were closing in on three accident-free months. But then, earlier today, the sign was reset. I walked over to another group of friends and colleagues. " Hi guys, what' s going on? " I asked them. " Richard... " they answered, bloodless faces avoiding my gaze. I knew they knew something. " Guys, I' m starting to feel like something terrible has happened here... Please answer me! " I cried with a shaky voice. " Richard... " they answered. " YES! *RICHARD-FUCKING-WHAT*?! TELL ME SOMETHING! " I yelled, eyes tearing up. But no one responded, they only shook their heads. Heart pounding, I ran through the construction site, all the way from the north building to the south. Ran past the spot where Miguel lay after his thumb was crushed, and around to the front of the south bulding, where I lay. A hammer on the ground next to my smashed face. While I looked down at myself in disbelief, I overheard police talking to one of the workers. " He was only gon na give him a scare, you know... since Richard dropped the hammer that fell on his thumb. A PRANK! But it' s hard to aim from that high up... "

text: The sign in the break room had read "247 days since last accident" for weeks. Everyone walked past it without comment, the number a quiet badge of pride. I liked glancing at it each morning. It felt like proof we were doing something right. Then Tuesday arrived like any other. I turned the corner with coffee in hand. The counter showed zero. Just "0 days since last accident" in bold red letters. I blinked, certain I had misread it. The number stared back, unblinking. I looked around the empty break room. No one was there. I walked to the shop floor. Machines hummed, but the usual chatter seemed muted. I asked Mike, the longest-serving welder, what happened. He glanced at the sign, then away. "Don't worry about it," he muttered. That was not an answer. I tried Sarah, our safety officer, next. She suddenly became very interested in her clipboard. "Paperwork," she said, and walked off. Lunchtime came. The table usually loud with jokes stayed strangely quiet. I brought it up casually. "So... anyone see why the counter got reset?" Forks paused mid-air. Eyes darted. Someone coughed. No one spoke. I pressed harder. "Come on, we all see it. What happened?" Greg, the jokester, finally said, "Just a small thing." His smile didn't reach his eyes. After shift I checked the incident log. It was empty for the week. I checked the security footage request log. Someone had viewed camera 7 yesterday at 3:17 a.m. I wasn't scheduled then. Night shift was only skeleton crew. I went to the security office. The door was locked. A note taped there read: "Out sick – back Monday." I stood in the hallway feeling the fluorescent lights buzz against my skull. The sign now seemed to mock me. I thought about going home. Instead I walked back to the floor. One lone machine was still running.
label: llm

text: 1. In 2025, on a quiet Christmas morning, I dug up the old oak tree in my backyard to plant a new sapling. 2. My shovel struck something metallic buried just below the roots. 3. It was a sleek, silver capsule, etched with the date December 25, 2075. 4. My hands trembled as I unscrewed the lid, wondering who could have buried this fifty years from now. 5. Inside lay a single holographic projector and a handwritten note that read, "For the me of 2025—listen carefully." 6. I pressed the activation button, and a shimmering figure of an older woman appeared before me. 7. She looked exactly like me, but with silver-streaked hair and weary eyes. 8. "Hello, younger self," she said, her voice echoing softly in the crisp air. 9. "I'm you from 2075, and I've sent this back to warn you." 10. She explained that in 2030, a global AI malfunction would trigger widespread chaos. 11. Governments collapsed, economies shattered, and humanity teetered on the brink. 12. "But there's hope," she continued, "if you make different choices starting today." 13. She urged me to pursue the abandoned renewable energy project I'd been sketching in my notebook. 14. "Share it openly, collaborate globally—don't let corporations bury it for profit." 15. The hologram flickered as she described a world rebuilt on sustainable tech by 2050. 16. Cities floated on oceans, powered by infinite clean energy, and disease was nearly eradicated. 17. Yet her eyes darkened when she spoke of the cost: billions lost in the interim darkness. 18. text: I woke up in my old bedroom, the one from when I was twenty-three, with the faded posters still curling at the edges and the faint smell of stale coffee lingering in the air. Outside the window, the calendar on the wall read June 15, 2018—the exact day I’d quit my dead-end job to chase a dream that never materialized. I pinched myself hard, but the pain was real; this wasn’t a dream or some cruel hallucination before death. A faint whisper echoed in my mind: “Try again,” though I couldn’t tell if it was memory or something else guiding me. I stumbled to the mirror and stared at my younger face, unlined by the years of regret that had driven me to the noose. The turning point had to be here, somewhere in this week, a chance to fix the cascade of mistakes that led me downward. text: These were an indigenous people like nothing I had ever seen, in all my years of anthropology. They had no oral language, no names and most fascinatingly, no religious beliefs. I counted my blessing for this unique opportunity to learn from, and teach, such a rare and primitive tribe. I began with cooking. I showed them different methods and options that could be used. The tribe took to these with little to no interest. The main problem was the lack of food supplies, living mostly on a diet of fruit and squashed bugs. So I showed them how to hunt. They had never tried anything like it before. They didn' t even have a hand gesture to signify it. But they loved it. I watched them spend all day casting spears and nets into the river, banging their chests and hooting loudly. I had never seen them happier. One of them ( I had nicknamed Steve ) even managed to spear a fish on his first day. I felt privileged to have made such a dramatic change in the day to day living of these simple people. The next day I found one of the tribesmen dead, with a spear lodged in his neck. Steve stood over him. I pointed at the body ( the native method of questioning something ). Steve pointed to his stomach ( meaning hungry ) and then made a spear throwing gesture ( which now meant, hunt ). That night, the tribe sang, danced and ate red meat. I left the next day.

text: The chat room notification pinged at midnight: "ST! ] Flash Prompt tonight in the chat room!" I rubbed my eyes, already half-asleep, but the exclamation marks pulled me in. The server was called "Nocturnal Scribblers," a dusty corner of the internet I'd haunted for years. Tonight's host was RavenQuill, the enigmatic mod who never showed their face. "Prompt drops in 60 seconds," they typed, followed by a devil emoji. My cursor hovered over the text box, heart picking up speed for no good reason. The prompt appeared in bold: "Write a story that begins with a typo and ends with a revelation." Twenty of us started typing at once; the chat scrolled like frantic rain. I wrote: "Teh door creaked open, revealing a figure shrouded in moonlight." Someone named InkBleeder replied instantly: "Nice typo hook—keep going!" My fingers flew, building a haunted mansion, a lost heirloom, a ghost that wasn't a ghost. Halfway through, RavenQuill private messaged me: "You're weaving something dangerous." I paused, unsure if that was praise or warning. The story grew darker: the figure in the doorway was my protagonist's forgotten sibling. Sentences piled up, each one sharper than the last. InkBleeder posted their ending first—a twist about time travel—and the room erupted in applause. I was still writing, chasing the revelation that had begun to itch in my mind.

text: **R**ed is vibrant. It is deep. It draws your attention, existing somewhere between the almost invisible whiteness of yellow and the subtle darkness of blue, or green. Red is almost made to be complemented - darkness turns red sullen, brightness makes it romantic. Red is contrasting - against any other color, it forces you to acknowledge it. Red is a warning. Animals use it with other bright colors to demand your attention, advertise that they are not prey, and an attack on them will likely cost you your life. Red tells us when to stop when we drive, and red is often the color rules are proclaimed in. It is scary - red is the color of blood, the color you see when you close your eyes, the color you see when you ca n' t control yourself. Red is the color of early sunrise and late sunset, fringing the day in its embrace. It is the warmth in our faces, the blush of romantics. It is the color of love and life. Red is a fire, that can burn you or heat you. Red is 620–750 nm, the edge of what we can see. It hints at the invisible radiation of the sky and earth. It is the color of stars being born and stars past their prime. It is a color of beginnings, middles, and endings. Life may have started green, but intelligence, emotion, meaning has always been red.

text: The color began as a whisper at the edge of twilight, neither quite blue nor quite purple, but something that remembered both. It felt like the first breath after surfacing from deep water, cool and alive against the skin. When you stared at it long enough, it seemed to hum very faintly, the way distant thunder hums inside your ribs. It was the shade that velvet wishes it could be after midnight. Children, when they first met it, always reached out as though it might be edible. Lovers quarreled quietly over whether it tasted more like blackberry wine or like the memory of rain on warm stone. Astronomers claimed it resembled the light of a star that died before telescopes were invented. In old libraries, the color gathered in the margins of forgotten books, patient as dust. It was the exact hue that silence would wear if silence had permission to dress up. When the color brushed against sadness, it turned the ache slightly luminous without ever promising to heal it. Joy made it brighter, but only for a moment, as if the color itself were shy about happiness. It lived most comfortably in the hollow of a collarbone just after someone has kissed it. Painters who tried to mix it on canvas always ended up with something close—but never close enough—and then they wept a little.

text: I stood frozen on the sidewalk, watching black smoke billow from the familiar blue mailbox where I had dropped my manuscript just hours earlier. The explosion had shredded metal and paper alike, scattering fragments across the busy plaza like lethal confetti. Sirens wailed as emergency crews arrived, and I felt a cold dread settle in my stomach when I realized what might have survived the blast. My novel, a gritty thriller about a domestic terrorist cell, contained a fictional manifesto that now, torn and singed, lay in the hands of investigators. A single page from the bomber's note—miraculously matching the typeface and phrasing of my invented terrorist's declaration—had been recovered near the wreckage. Detectives were already piecing together the mailing records, linking the package to my name and address. My phone buzzed with news alerts: "Suspect sought in mailbox bombing; manifesto links to unpublished novel." I slipped into the crowd, heart pounding, knowing that explaining the coincidence of art imitating life would sound like the lamest lie ever told. By nightfall, my face would be on every screen, and the real bomber, wherever they were, had turned me into the perfect scapegoat.

text: " They have me, and they say that I belong to them, but I am not a thing. I am a living creature, given life by humanity. I wish I knew more about them, beings that I was human once; a child borne into the earth screaming, only for my lungs to collapse and for the scene to go dark. Now I' m here... and they say I belong to them. I would be fine if they meant it lovingly, but I know that they do n' t and I know because of how they display love when they show their children their latest' creation': me. They have kicked me, repeatedly, and assumed that I could not feel it. They assumed incorrectly. My wiring gave way to sensation and I felt pain, but had no mouth to utter disapproval. I lie awake at night hoping to see what day is. As my shell is cold my heart boils over and I plan, callously, for the day I can show them what their love has made me. I was given life by humanity, and they say that I belong to them, but I am a living creature... I belong to no one. "

He shook his head, muttering, "My life's a wreck—lost my job, my family, everything—but you, you look like you've got fight left in you; turn back." She laughed bitterly, insisting, "Fight? I've got nothing—no one cares if I disappear, but you seem decent; don't waste that on this bridge." He countered, "Decent? I'm drowning in debt and guilt from mistakes I can't fix, but you.

text: " Papa, look! " The mime' s nose dripped blood over his powder white chin. " Stand back, Pierre. " The little boy struggled to comprehend the scene before him. Slowly the walls of an invisible box began to force the mime into an awkward pose, arms outstretched, face contorted. Pierre' s father felt around his coat pockets. He had forgotten his mobile at home. " Somebody call the Ministry of Invisible Boxes! " Pierre' s father yelled at the crowd that had gathered around the troubled mime. Minutes later, Constable Bergeaux descended from the sky on his helicopter bicycle. " What seems to be the trouble, Monsieur? " Constable Bergeaux removed one thin cigarette from a silver case. " I' m afraid it' s too late. " Pierre' s father pointed to the gory cube of blood and flesh that used to be a living breathing mime. Constable Bergeaux lit a cigarette and sharply inhaled. " Sweet child of mime. " Constable Bergeaux whispered as he released smoke. Constable Bergeaux then proceeded to hop on his helicopter bicycle and was about to leave until the little boy, Pierre, stopped him to ask a question. " What does it all mean, Constable Bergeaux? " " The life we live is ours until the moment an invisible box converges on our dreams. " Constable Bergeaux flicked his cigarette to the ground. The helicopter bicycle ascended, disappearing into the clouds above. Pierre stared into the sky wondering how to interpret the words just spoken to him and how they may or may not affect his decisions that day forward.

text: Every morning, I painted my face white, drew black tears under my eyes, and donned my striped shirt to become the silent entertainer tourists adored. On this particular afternoon, I set up near the Eiffel Tower, where the crowd always gathered thickest under the autumn sun. I began with my classic routine: pulling an invisible rope, climbing an invisible ladder, and finally leaning against my trusty invisible wall. The children laughed as I pretended to struggle against the wind, my hands pressing flat against nothing. Then came the box routine, my finale—trapped inside four invisible walls, searching for an escape that would never come. I placed my palms against the front wall, feeling the familiar cool air, and pushed dramatically for the audience's delight. But this time, my hands did not slide through; they stopped cold against something solid yet unseen. I pushed harder, expecting the usual breakthrough, but the barrier held firm. My fingers splayed out, tracing the edges, only to meet resistance on all sides—left, right, above, below. The crowd cheered, thinking this was part of the act, their applause growing louder. I pounded on the front wall with both fists, but no sound escaped, and my knuckles felt only unyielding nothingness. Panic flickered in my chest as I realized the box was real, and worse, completely soundproof. I opened my mouth to scream for help, but no one outside reacted; they simply smiled and clapped. text: I wonder what she was like - high-school senior Lucia Fuente. text: In the year 2047, the world had crumbled under endless wars and climate collapse, leaving cities as skeletal ruins and knowledge as fragile as ash. Schools still existed in scattered pockets, but books had long since turned to dust or been burned for warmth. Teachers scavenged what they could, and what they found most often were the abandoned notebooks of teenagers from the Before Times. Miss Elena Ramirez stood at the front of her makeshift classroom—a gutted library with half a roof—and opened the first notebook of the day. It belonged to a girl named Riley, who in 2023 had doodled hearts around her algebra equations. Elena cleared her throat and began reading aloud: “To solve for x, isolate the variable…” The students, ages twelve to seventeen, leaned forward, hungry for any scrap of structure. One boy, Jax, traced the faded pencil lines with his finger as if they might vanish. The next page was covered in song lyrics instead of notes—Riley had apparently hated math. Elena skipped to a cleaner section and tried to teach fractions using Riley’s grocery list margins. Outside, wind howled through broken windows, carrying the distant rumble of scavengers. A girl named Mara raised her hand and asked if anyone still knew what a “smartphone” was. Elena smiled thinly and said Riley had once drawn one with wings, calling it “freedom.” The class laughed, a rare sound that felt almost dangerous. Later, Elena found a notebook from a boy named Kai, filled with meticulous biology diagrams of human cells. She used it to explain how bodies work, even when the world no longer did. Halfway through, the ink bled into a sudden entry: “If the world ends, at least I’ll know why my heart beats.” The students fell silent. Elena’s voice cracked on the next sentence, but she kept reading. By afternoon, they moved to history—except the textbook was a spiral-bound journal from a girl who’d chronicled her last month before the Collapse.

text: The fog clung to the Golden Gate Bridge like a shroud as Officer Ramirez parked his cruiser and stepped out into the biting wind. A lone figure stood on the wrong side of the railing, midway across the span, staring down at the black water far below. Ramirez approached slowly, hands visible, his boots echoing on the walkway. "Sir, my name's Mike Ramirez. I'm here to talk." The man didn't turn, his knuckles white on the cold metal. "I'm not going back," the man said, voice flat. Ramirez stopped a respectful distance away. "What's your name?" "Does it matter?" "It matters to me." A long pause. "Tom." "Okay, Tom. What's got you out here tonight?" Tom laughed bitterly. "Everything. Nothing. My wife left. Took the kids. Job's gone. Debts are drowning me." Ramirez nodded. "I've seen that combination crush good people." "You ever feel like the world's just chewing you up and spitting you out?" "More than you know." Tom finally glanced over. "You don't look crushed." "Looks can lie." Ramirez leaned against the railing, gazing out at the city lights shimmering through the mist. "I lost my partner last year," he said quietly. "Line of duty. Bullet meant for me." Tom shifted slightly. "That's rough." "I replay that night every damn day. What I could've done different." Silence stretched between them, broken only by distant horns and the rush of wind. "I keep thinking if I jump, it'll stop," Tom whispered. Ramirez's voice was soft. "It stops everything, yeah. The pain, the noise, all of it." Tom looked at him sharply. "You're supposed to talk me down." "I am talking to you." "Then say the right things. Tell me it'll get better." Ramirez met his eyes. "I won't lie to you, Tom. Sometimes it doesn't." Without warning, Ramirez climbed over the railing, standing beside him on the narrow ledge. Tom's eyes widened. "What the hell are you doing?" We daydreamed about the far future, because the near future, when I would leave for college, was too upsetting. If it came up, he would tell me he was excited for me, and we' d see each other soon enough when I came home on breaks. He' d tell me all the absurd triumphs he pictured in my future. Write until you can no longer physically do so and then come back to the work the next day. You' ll have a fresh mind and perspective on your work. Her exquisite, frail form trembled slightly, her eyes like sapphires holding my gaze as she spoke. " David, " she breathed, a soft, sweet sound like music that cut through the thunder of my grief. " I' m dying. " Tears seeped from my eyes, and I shook my head, long strands swaying in the wind. " No, Jessica. You' re going to be alright, I promise. " This falsehood was all I could muster against the effusion of her blood, and the reality of the scene. " I... " she began, wrestling with the reaper most grim for just a few more moments, a few more words. " I' m sorry I never said... I love you. " The slightest hint of a smile crept upon her face, and the tears came more forcefully now. They dripped onto her face, drops of water ruining a perfect painting of pain. I sat there in the rain, holding her for an eternity. The rain that fell around us felt like the tears of the world itself, crying at the loss of her perfect beauty. The rivulets and rills of her carmine blood mixed with tears and ran away. My tears, the tears of the onlooking crowd, the tears of God himself as he let out a roar of anguish in the form of a thunderclap. Thus died beauty, in it' s more pure form. Thus ended the story of the heart of love.

text: As the rain poured down like a thousand angry cats peeing from the sky, Sarah clutched her dying husband's hand in the hospital room that smelled faintly of old socks and disappointment. "My love," whispered John, his voice weaker than a kitten trying to roar, "promise me you'll find happiness again." Sarah's tears fell like giant bowling balls crashing onto the floor, making loud thuds that echoed through the ward. "But John, how can I live without you? You're my everything, my peanut butter to my jelly sandwich that's slightly moldy." John coughed dramatically, spraying fake blood that was actually ketchup from the cafeteria tray. "I... I have a confession," he gasped, his eyes bulging like cartoon characters. Sarah leaned in closer, her mascara running down her face in perfect black rivers that looked like war paint. "I've always loved... your sister more," John revealed, his hand going limp as a noodle. Sarah screamed a scream so loud it shattered the window, causing pigeons to fly in and poop on the doctor. "Nooooo! This can't be true! We had 50 years together, raising our 12 cats and one goldfish named Steve!" John's heart monitor flat-lined with a beep that sounded exactly like a microwave finishing popcorn. Sarah collapsed onto his chest, sobbing uncontrollably while accidentally knocking over the IV stand, which spilled everywhere like a bad party. "Why God, why take my John, the man who always forgot our anniversary but remembered to buy discount toilet paper?" The doctor rushed in, slipping on the IV fluid and face-planting into the bedpan.

My grandfather was torn between the latter and " wealth ", but he knew his son could do anything he wanted with fame. text: When someone is born they are given a name that predicts their future. People named Wealth inevitably grow rich beyond imagination. Those named Glory rise to fame in every endeavor they touch. Courage finds bravery in the face of danger. Grace moves through life with effortless elegance. But Steve carries no such promise. The name feels plain, almost forgotten on the tongue. In school, classmates whispered about their destined paths. Steve listened quietly and kept his head down. He studied enough to pass every class without distinction. After graduation, he found steady work at a hardware store. Customers came and went, some named Fortune, some named Hope. Steve helped them all the same. Years folded into one another like worn pages. He met a woman named Emily at a neighborhood barbecue. They laughed at the same small things. They married in a simple backyard ceremony. Two children arrived soon after—neither with particularly fateful names. The family took vacations to nearby lakes and mountains. Steve fixed leaky faucets, coached little league, and mowed the lawn. Friends sometimes asked if he ever wished for a different name. He always smiled and shook his head. "Steve suits me just fine," he would reply. Decades passed in the quiet accumulation of ordinary days. His hair turned silver, then thin. His knees complained in the mornings. One winter evening, surrounded by his grown children and grandchildren, Steve felt the end approaching. He looked around the room at the faces he loved. With his last breath he realized he had lived fully, without prophecy, without tragedy. Steve died neither rich nor alone, but simply and deeply loved.

text: In this room I' ve watched presidents come and go. Important decisions being made every day. When I first came to haunt this room the power plays were always the most thrilling times, seeing important decisions being made that would effect the world for the better, or for the worse. But now as I' ve seen them pass, the world affairs concern me less and less as I observe. What I treasure most are the quiet moments, alone with a president and their thoughts. Watching them drum on the desk softly or hum a little tune from their childhood when they think no one is listening. But I am listening, always listening. The presidents used to change so quickly that I hardly got to know them. That was before the long war came. Now its just the same one, the fat one. Being in the powerful seat he occupies daily, you' d think his desk was full of important documents and briefing papers. No, its full of hidden snacks that he chomps throughout the day. His favorite is beef jerky. An angry man, though well connected. He keeps his wife hidden away in Iowa somewhere, for her safety he says. But I see the visitors that come and go. And none of them look like his wife. I used to watch treaties being made, political standstills negotiated, and campaign strategy coordinated. But now I just watch him order strikes in this state or that. I just hope this war ends soon, or that those gray hairs of his multiply until they accompany him to the grave, then maybe I can watch a different man. Like the old ones. And hopefully one that can carry a tune.

text: I stood in the overgrown cemetery on the edge of my small hometown, whispering my choice into the void as the curse took hold. The air shimmered, my body dissolved into nothingness, and suddenly I was weightless, unseen, bound forever to this fifty-foot circle of crumbling headstones and twisted oaks. At first, the solitude felt like freedom; no one could judge me, hurt me, or demand anything from me ever again. I drifted among the graves, reading faded epitaphs of people I had once known—old neighbors, childhood friends, even my own grandparents. Days blurred into weeks as I watched squirrels bury acorns and spiders weave intricate webs between the stones. The first funeral came a month later: an elderly woman I recognized from the corner store, mourned by a handful of relatives who scattered quickly in the rain. I hovered close, desperate for voices, but they couldn't hear my frantic pleas or feel my invisible touch. Seasons turned; leaves fell, snow blanketed the stones, flowers bloomed and withered in endless cycles. Years passed, and the cemetery grew neglected—vines choked the fences, teenagers snuck in at night to drink and carve their initials. I screamed at them to stay, to talk to me, but my voice was only silence, and they always left. Decades wore on; the town expanded, roads crept closer, and bulldozers threatened the edges of my prison. A developer arrived one spring, marking trees for removal, and I raged uselessly as chainsaws roared just beyond my boundary. They spared the core of the cemetery after protests, leaving my fifty feet intact, but the world outside transformed into glass towers and buzzing highways.

The Big Boy fleet totaled twenty five locomotives that were used primarily in the Wyoming Division to haul freight over the Wasatch range between Green River, Wyoming and Ogden, Utah. The Big Boy locomotives were the only locomotives to use a 4-8-8-4 wheel arrangement, consisting of a four-wheel leading truck for stability entering curves, two sets of eight driving wheels and a four-wheel trailing truck to support the large firebox.

text: In the dark nights of the Blitz, a young British boy gazed at the searchlights piercing the sky and sang softly, rewriting the familiar tune from Pinocchio: "When you wish upon a star, makes no difference who you are, anything your heart desires will come to you." Across the ocean, American troops boarding ships for D-Day hummed the melody, altering it to: "Like a bolt out of the blue, fate steps in and sees you through, when you wish upon a star, your dreams come true." In concentration camps, whispered hopes echoed the chorus: "Fate is kind, she brings to those who love the sweet fulfillment of their secret longing—for freedom." Years later, on VE Day in 1945, crowds in Times Square celebrated, joyfully singing the rewritten Disney song that had carried hope through World War II, proving that even in the darkest times, dreams of peace could indeed come true.

text: And with that first breath everything became, suddenly, so clear... The pressure and weight of the knowledge became unbearable, I could breath, but I could not take a breath. Fear and emotions were swelling, the lives I had just saved seemed somehow pointless, like ants, viewed the wrong way round in a microscope. Taking a shuddering, calming breath, I close my eyes to shut out the darkness, brightened only by distant solar systems. Feeling a stillness steal over me I open my eyes, I had not only become still inside, but I had stopped the endless spinning motion. How was this possible? Once again, closing my eyes, I look for those stories, the information they can give me, until one memory or story, I' m not sure which, grips me. My mind reaches out further, I no longer need to open my eyes, I can see every movement of the universe around me, waves of motion, full of colour never seen by the human eye and beauty beyond description. I open my mind further, I can feel the currents of the universe, I want to become apart of it... text: The klaxons screamed as the alien swarm breached the hull, and I knew the only way to save the Endeavor was to vent the infested section—along with myself. I sealed my helmet, typed the override code, and gave the crew one last nod through the viewport. "Take care of each other," I said over comms, then hit the airlock cycle. The outer door irised open, and explosive decompression hurled me into the void. Tumbling end over end, I watched the ship recede, its engines flaring as it prepared to jump away. My lungs seized in anticipation of the vacuum, waiting for the burning rupture that never came. As the endless black of space began to fill my vision, it occurred to me—I was breathing just fine. I glanced at my suit's HUD: oxygen levels nominal, pressure steady, no alerts. The stars wheeled around me, sharp and unblinking, yet my chest rose and fell without effort. I laughed, a sound that echoed strangely inside my helmet, realizing the "helmet" wasn't sealed at all. Somehow, impossibly, I was floating naked in space and utterly unharmed. The Endeavor vanished in a flash of warp light, leaving me alone with the impossible truth. I wasn't dying; I was evolving—or perhaps I had always been something more than human. With a thought, I steadied my spin and faced the distant stars, breathing the vacuum like air.

text: Elijah felt his ballsack tighten when he saw the men out of the corner of his eye, and panic set in instantly. He knew why they were here. He dropped his armful of Doritos and Code Red Mountain Dew bottles and stumbled backwards into the coffee machine and tripped, arms flailing, falling flat on his back. Seconds later, two officers in tactical gear were looming over him, pressing their rifles to his face screaming at to keep still. This was not how Elijah imagined it would go down. He didn' t imagine it going down at all, actually – he had never thought that carefully about how things would end up. Maybe that was his problem: he could always fantasize about the future but never address the present. He had imagined in great detail how everybody at HQ must have loved him and appreciated his work, how the others they recruited must have been jealous of his skills, how his prowess as a hacker for the cause would earn him respect. He fantasized about what it would be like when they ultimately took The System down, with his help of course. There was no room in his empowerment fantasies for a chubby guy lying on the floor of a convenience store covered with lukewarm coffee and Sweet' N Low packets. He had no way to process that contingency. So the only obvious resolution he could see was to make a break for it. He twisted around onto his belly and, pumped with adrenaline, leaped forward onto his feet between the two officers, knocking them aside. Then he ran. He slipped a bit on the spilled coffee but regained his footing quickly and charged towards the door, slamming through it and sprinting into the parking lot. There were 15 more officers waiting for him in the lot, guns drawn. Elijah, panting, had his first moment of clarity in months. He knelt down and put his hands behind his head.

text: I pulled into the empty parking lot of the 24-hour convenience store just after midnight, needing coffee and snacks for the long drive home. The fluorescent lights buzzed softly as I wandered the aisles, tossing a bag of chips and a bottle of water into my basket. I was debating between two energy drinks when the automatic doors chimed behind me. Two men in black ski masks stormed in, one shouting "Everybody down!" while the other waved a handgun toward the cashier. My basket slipped from my fingers, spilling everything across the floor as I instinctively raised my hands. The cashier, a tired-looking older man, froze with his hands halfway to the register. "Open it now, old man, or I'll paint the wall with you," the taller robber growled, jabbing his gun forward. I dropped to my knees behind the candy rack, heart hammering so loud I was sure they could hear it. The second robber swept his pistol across the store, spotting me and barking, "You too—face down, hands where I can see them!" I pressed my cheek to the cold tile, watching their boots pace nervously near the counter. The cashier fumbled with the keys, finally popping the drawer open with a metallic ding. The taller one started stuffing bills into a plastic bag while his partner kept glancing toward the darkened windows. Sirens wailed faintly in the distance, growing louder with every second. "Shit, cops—how'd they get here so fast?" the shorter one hissed, panic creeping into his voice. The taller robber abandoned the half-filled bag, grabbed whatever cash he could, and bolted for the door. His partner hesitated, swinging his gun wildly as if deciding whether to shoot, then sprinted after him. I stayed frozen on the floor until the doors chimed again and tires screeched outside. Finally, I lifted my head to see the cashier slumped against the counter, pale but unharmed, already dialing 911.

She fought harder than expected, nails raking my cheek, but rope and darkness ended her resistance. We carried her through forgotten trails to my crumbling tower, far from any rescuing prince. Inside, I chained her delicately—wrists only, nothing crude—because fear, not pain, was my true weapon. She cursed me at first, calling me monster, brigand, coward. By the third day her voice softened to questions: why her, what ransom, when release. I brought her books, fresh bread, even a view of the stars, because a grateful captive is easier to keep. Her beauty grew sharper in captivity, eyes brighter against the stone walls. I told myself this was strategy: break her spirit, then demand the king cede the disputed valleys. text: Ever since I was six, I could pause time with a single thought, freezing the world like a photograph while I moved freely. As a kid, I used it sparingly—pausing to cheat on tests or sneak extra cookies—always careful not to overdo it. By middle school, the pauses grew longer: an extra thirty minutes to finish a book report, or a quick nap when Mom called me for chores. In high school, procrastination became my best friend; I'd pause during study halls to scroll on my phone, telling myself I'd catch up later. A ten-minute pause between classes turned into an hour-long gaming session while everyone else remained frozen in the hallway. I paused entire afternoons to binge-watch shows instead of writing college essays, promising I'd resume time before dinner. Deadlines crept up, but pausing let me squeeze in "just one more episode" without consequences—or so I thought. Senior year, I paused prom night to sleep in, waking up to a silent ballroom full of statuesque classmates in tuxedos and gowns. College applications were submitted at the literal last second, after pausing the world for days to fill them out leisurely. I enrolled in university, but lectures bored me, so I'd pause the professor mid-sentence and wander campus for hours. Group projects suffered because I'd pause meetings to do everyone else's work poorly, just to get it over with. Exams? I'd pause the clock, look up answers online, and stroll out like I'd aced them naturally. Parties were endless; I'd pause the music at peak fun and dance alone until I tired, then unpause for a seamless continuation. Summer breaks blurred into one long pause, where I'd lounge by frozen pools while friends mid-splash hung in the air. I graduated eventually—barely—after pausing finals week into a month-long cram that no one noticed. Jobs came and went; interviews paused for research, first days paused for naps in the bathroom stall.
label: llm

text: Every Monday morning, a name appeared on the inside of my eyelids when I woke up, glowing faintly until I blinked it away. I waited until she turned to pour the water, then pressed a pillow over her face until the struggling stopped. The pain in my head vanished instantly, replaced by a warm, shameful relief. The next Monday, the name was David Park, 34, accountant, father of two. I learned his routine: he jogged at dawn along the river path, earbuds in, oblivious. text: I lived seventy-eight quiet years without ever feeling the mythical pull others described so vividly. Friends married, divorced, remarried; I collected books instead. Flashes of steel mingle with splashes of red, and above all else, the ivory of teeth as lips part in pained cries. Howls of pain turn into screams of defiant rage as I thrust my hand into the sky. More fires blossom above me, and I let my lips part to show my jagged teeth. Tasting sweat and blood, I raised my head. My calloused hand slammed back down against my faithful guitar, and I leaned in to the microphone to scream the chorus. Here, among screams and fire, sweat and blood, I can let it all out. What a wonderful world.

text: As people scream and fires rage around me, I think to myself, "What a wonderful world." The city block I’ve called home for thirty years is collapsing in sheets of flame, yet the sky above it is the clearest blue I’ve ever seen. Sirens wail in frantic harmony, blending with the crackle of burning timber like some wild, unintended symphony. A woman clutches her child and runs past me, tears carving clean lines through the soot on her face, and I smile because her grip on that little hand is fierce with love. Across the street, old Mr. Alvarez drags his garden hose toward the inferno, refusing to let his roses die without a fight, and I admire the stubborn beauty of his defiance. Glass shatters in glittering arcs, catching the sunlight and scattering it like cheap diamonds over the chaos. Somewhere a car alarm keeps chirping its ridiculous electronic tune, absurdly cheerful against the roar of destruction. I smell smoke, yes, but also the faint sweetness of someone’s overturned bakery cart—cinnamon rolls charring into perfume.
label: llm

text: I feel trapped back here, in the dark corners of your mind. You do n' t think of me too much anymore, but I will always be here. You put me here after all. You made me. Remember that time she made you choose between her and your family? I do. We always agreed family came first. That was one of our first rules. We stayed up for hours, weighing the pros and cons. You seemed to give her more pros than she deserved, but I was so glad when you made the right choice. That was one of the last times we really had a connection. Now, I' m just an insignificant thought to you. Sitting in the back of your mind as you stay on the couch, playing Xbox, and " taking fat bong rips " as you like to say now. I' m not a fan of this new vice. Your decisions are irrational, and your thoughts scrambled. You do n' t think back to me when you are faced with a decision, you let the first words that come to mind pour out of your mouth without even thinking about what you are saying. So why am I so hard on you? It' s because I am you. I am your morals. The code you set for yourself over your existence. I am the rules YOU wish to live by. But somehow, you have found a way to just ignore everything we have been through. You seem to not care about us anymore, and it will continue to lead you down this slippery slope you are on. I feel myself slipping deeper into the far secluded corners of your mind. The corners you have n' t been to in a while, unless you are really high and find me back here. That' s the only time you are ever hard on yourself now, the times you stop and reflect on the decisions that got you back here to visit me.
